```{r gam-rain-effect-time, fig.width=11, fig.height=6.5, dpi=300}
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey92", color = NA),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )
```

### Interpretation rain duration effects (7-day lag)

In contrast to temperature, the partial effect plots for rain duration show no strong or consistent association with wastewater viral load across the four virus targets once long-term temporal dynamics are accounted for.

For **Influenza A** and **SARS-CoV-2**, the estimated smooths suggest a weak negative association at higher rain durations. For **Influenza B**, the relationship is non-linear with declining viral load at higher rain durations. In contrast, **RSV** shows a weak positive trend.

Across all viruses, confidence intervals widen substantially at longer rain durations, reflecting sparse data for days with prolonged rainfall. This high uncertainty limits interpretability and indicates that the estimated effects are not robust.

Overall, rain duration does not appear to exert a systematic independent influence on wastewater viral load. The weak and inconsistent trends observed are likely driven by variability and limited observations rather than a causal rainfall-related mechanism.

**Interpretation**

The GAM analysis highlights that:

- Air temperature has a clear within-season association with wastewater viral load for **Influenza A**, **Influenza B**, and **RSV**.
- This effect represents seasonal amplification rather than temperature-driven outbreak initiation.
- Rain duration shows weak, inconsistent, and highly uncertain effects across all viruses.
- **SARS-CoV-2** differs from seasonal respiratory viruses by exhibiting weaker temperature dependence and minimal rainfall sensitivity.

It is important to emphasize that the GAMs are not forecasting models. They are designed to explain observed variation by separating long-term trends from short-term associations. As such, the models describe how weather variables modulate viral load within observed periods rather than predicting future epidemic dynamics.

Overall, the GAMs provide a flexible and interpretable framework to distinguish seasonal structure from short-term weather modulation, complementing the wave onset detection and scenario-based modelling presented before.

## Chapter of Choice: Wave onset detection in wastewater time series with Plotly

In this chapter, we focus on detecting and visualizing wastewater viral load time series, so-called wave onsets. In the previous sections, we analysed seasonal patterns and weather effects. Here, the goal is to identify when sustained growth begins before a major viral peak.

Wave onsets are not treated as single days, but as periods with continuously increasing viral load. We use this concept because wastewater data is noisy and it is difficult to define one exact start date. Instead of selecting one specific day, we define onset zones that describe a positive trend before a larger wave starts.

We visualize these onset zones using Plotly, an interactive visualization library for R. We chose this as our chapter of choice because interactive plots are especially helpful for long and noisy time series. They allow users to zoom in, move along the timeline, and inspect values in detail. This makes it easier to explore the data and better understand how the detected onset zones relate to the observed viral peaks. Users also have the option to hide a virus by clicking on its name in the legend on the right side. This allows them to focus only on the viruses they are interested in and makes it easier to compare specific time series without distraction.

All four viruses are shown in aligned time series with the same time axis, which allows direct comparison between virus targets. The detected onset zones are added as shaded areas, linking the statistical detection of onsets with the visual interpretation of the time series.

All analyses use the 7-day rolling mean (`value_mean7d`) to smooth the data and reduce noise and missing values. The viral load is square-root transformed (`sqrt(value)`) to keep zero values while making the variance more stable. Wave onsets are defined as periods with a sustained positive trend, based on rolling linear slopes, so short-term fluctuations are not mistaken for real onsets.

The detection is implemented as a function (`detect_wave_onset_zones`) that looks at each virus separately and orders the data by date. Larger waves are identified using a high quantile threshold (`high_quantile`) to define major waves. This ensures that only clearly elevated circulation phases are considered while avoiding sensitivity to minor fluctuations. For each detected wave, a fixed time window before the wave is analysed (pre_window_days = 60). Within this window, rolling linear slopes are calculated (`trend_window`) and consecutive positive slopes above a minimum threshold (`min_slope`) are used to define possible onset zones (`min_zone_length`).

To avoid false positives, we apply a simple validation step. The average viral load after an onset zone must be higher than during the zone (`mean_post > mean_zone`), otherwise the zone is removed. Overall, this approach focuses on continuous epidemic growth and links statistical detection with what can be seen in the time series.

```{r define-detect-wave-onset-zones, message=FALSE}
detect_wave_onset_zones <- function(data, virus_name,
                                    high_quantile = 0.80,
                                    min_high_duration = 14,
                                    trend_window = 7,
                                    min_slope = 0.005,
                                    pre_window_days = 60,
                                    min_zone_length = 7) {

  # prepare time series
  df <- data %>%
    dplyr::filter(value_category == virus_name) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(date) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      date = as.Date(date),
      y = sqrt(as.numeric(value_mean7d))
    ) %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(y))

  if (nrow(df) < 40) {
    return(list(df = df, zones = tibble::tibble()))
  }

  # define major waves (sustained high phase)
  threshold <- stats::quantile(df$y, high_quantile, na.rm = TRUE)

  df <- df %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      high_phase = y >= threshold,
      phase_id = with(rle(high_phase),
                      rep(seq_along(lengths), lengths))
    )

  waves <- df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(phase_id) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      is_wave    = first(high_phase),
      wave_start = first(date),
      duration   = dplyr::n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::filter(is_wave, duration >= min_high_duration) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(wave_start)

  if (nrow(waves) == 0) {
    return(list(df = df, zones = tibble::tibble()))
  }

  # STEP B: detect onset zones before each wave
  zones_list <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(waves)), function(i) {

    df_pre <- df %>%
      dplyr::filter(date < waves$wave_start[i]) %>%
      tail(pre_window_days)

    if (nrow(df_pre) < trend_window) return(NULL)

    df_pre <- df_pre %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        slope = zoo::rollapply(
          y,
          width = trend_window,
          align = "right",
          fill  = NA,
          FUN = function(y_win)
            coef(lm(y_win ~ seq_along(y_win)))[2]
        ),
        pos_trend = !is.na(slope) & slope > min_slope,
        run_id = with(rle(pos_trend),
                      rep(seq_along(lengths), lengths))
      )

    zones_i <- df_pre %>%
      dplyr::group_by(run_id) %>%
      dplyr::summarise(
        is_zone    = first(pos_trend),
        zone_start = first(date),
        zone_end   = last(date),
        duration   = dplyr::n(),
        mean_slope = mean(slope, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      ) %>%
      dplyr::filter(is_zone, duration >= min_zone_length)

    if (nrow(zones_i) == 0) return(NULL)

    # VALIDATION: must actually rise AFTER the zone
    zones_i <- zones_i %>%
      dplyr::rowwise() %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        mean_during = mean(
          df$y[df$date >= zone_start & df$date <= zone_end],
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
        mean_after = mean(
          df$y[df$date > zone_end & df$date <= zone_end + 14],
          na.rm = TRUE
        ),
        valid_onset = mean_after > mean_during
      ) %>%
      dplyr::ungroup() %>%
      dplyr::filter(valid_onset)

    if (nrow(zones_i) == 0) return(NULL)

    # take the last valid zone before the wave
    zones_i %>% dplyr::slice_tail(n = 1)
  })

  list(
    df    = df,
    zones = dplyr::bind_rows(zones_list)
  )
}
```

We use the same detection for all viruses, but we run it separately for each virus (`virus_name`). This is important because the viruses behave differently over time and need slightly different settings, for example for the high quantile (`high_quantile`) or the minimum length of a wave (`min_high_duration`). By doing this, each virus is analysed individually and the detection can be adapted to its specific dynamics, rather than applying the same fixed parameters to all viruses.

The method is run in a loop over all viruses (`virus_map`). For each virus, the wave detection function (`detect_wave_onset_zones()`) is applied using the matching value category (`value_category`).

The results are stored together (`results`) and then merged into one dataset for the time series (`ts_all`) and one for the onset zones (`zones_all`). This makes it possible to plot all viruses in the same way and compare them directly later on.

```{r wave-zones-build, message=FALSE}
virus_map <- tibble::tibble(
  virus = c("Influenza A", "Influenza B", "RSV", "SARS-CoV-2"),
  value_category = c("influenza_a", "influenza_b",  "respiratory_syncytial_virus" , "sars-cov-2")
)

results <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(virus_map)), function(i) {

  v  <- virus_map$virus[i]
  vc <- virus_map$value_category[i]

  detect_wave_onset_zones(
    data = final_dataset_analysis,
    virus_name = vc,
    high_quantile      = ifelse(v == "SARS-CoV-2", 0.75, 0.80),
    min_high_duration  = ifelse(v %in% c("Influenza B", "RSV", "SARS-CoV-2"), 10, 14),
    trend_window       = 7,
    min_slope          = ifelse(v == "SARS-CoV-2", 0.004, 0.005),
    pre_window_days    = 60,
    min_zone_length    = 7
  )
})

# build panel datasets
ts_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(results), function(i) {
  results[[i]]$df %>%
    mutate(virus = virus_map$virus[i])
}))

zones_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(results), function(i) {
  results[[i]]$zones %>%
    mutate(virus = virus_map$virus[i])
}))
```

All plots use the same time axis and can be explored interactively.

This makes it easier to see how the detections fit the data. Early increases are easier to spot, and differences in timing and wave patterns between viruses become clearer.

```{r wave-onset-zones-panel-plotly, echo=FALSE, fig.height=13, fig.width=8.5}

virus_order <- c("Influenza A", "Influenza B", "RSV", "SARS-CoV-2")

virus_colors <- c(
  "Influenza A" = "#1b9e77",
  "Influenza B" = "#7570b3",
  "RSV"         = "#e7298a",
  "SARS-CoV-2"  = "#d95f02"
)

plots <- lapply(virus_order, function(v) {

  ts_v    <- ts_all    %>% filter(virus == v)
  zones_v <- zones_all %>% filter(virus == v)

  p <- plotly::plot_ly(
    data = ts_v,
    x = ~date,
    y = ~y,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    name = paste0(v, " – Viral load (7-day mean, sqrt)"),
    line = list(color = virus_colors[[v]], width = 1.2),
    showlegend = TRUE,  
    hovertemplate =
      "<b>Date:</b> %{x}<br><b>sqrt(load):</b> %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"
  )

  # Onset-Zonen
  if (nrow(zones_v) > 0) {
    p <- plotly::layout(
      p,
      shapes = lapply(seq_len(nrow(zones_v)), function(i) {
        list(
          type = "rect",
          xref = "x",
          yref = "paper",
          x0 = zones_v$zone_start[i],
          x1 = zones_v$zone_end[i],
          y0 = 0,
          y1 = 1,
          fillcolor = "rgba(215,48,39,0.25)",
          line = list(width = 0)
        )
      })
    )
  }

  plotly::layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = v, x = 0),
    yaxis = list(title = "sqrt(value_mean7d)")
  )
})

plotly::subplot(
  plots,
  nrows = 4,
  shareX = TRUE,
  titleX = TRUE
) %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "<b>Detected onset zones of major wastewater viral load waves</b><br>",
        "<span style='font-size:12px'>Pink shaded areas indicate sustained positive trends preceding major waves.</span>"
      ),
      x = 0
    ),
    legend = list(
      orientation = "v",
      x = 1.02,
      y = 1,
      traceorder = "normal"
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Date",
      rangeslider = list(visible = TRUE)
    ),
    hovermode = "x unified",
    dragmode = "zoom",
    margin = list(l = 85, r = 180, t = 110, b = 80)
  )
```

**Interpretation**

In the sections before, we looked at seasonal patterns, weather effects, and the detected onset zones (`zones_all`). Up to now, the whole time series (`final_dataset_analysis`) was analysed as one continuous timeline, without clearly separating different phases of a wave.

Here, we take the detected onset zones and split the waves into three phases (`wave_phase`) to look at viral load and weather conditions in more detail:

- **Pre-onset phase** (`wave_phase = "Pre-growth"`): the time before an onset zone, when viral load is still low

- **Onset phase** (`wave_phase = "Growth"`): the onset zone itself, where the viral load starts to increase consistently based on short-term trends (`slope_7d`)

- **Post-onset phase** (`wave_phase = "High-load"`): the period after the onset zone, usually with high or peak viral load (`quantile(sqrt(value_mean7d), 0.75`))

The phase classification is based on short-term changes in the viral load. These trends are calculated using a rolling linear slope over seven days (`rollapply, width = 7`) applied to the square-root transformed viral load (`sqrt(value_mean7d)`).

This way, we can compare early wave development with later stages. The analysis directly uses the previously detected onset zones (`detect_wave_onset_zones()`) and does not add any new detection rules.

```{r wave-phase-construction, message=FALSE}
# Construct wave-phase labels based on detected onset zones

wave_phase_df <- final_dataset_analysis %>%
  arrange(value_category, date) %>%
  group_by(value_category) %>%
  mutate(
    # short-term trend using rolling linear slope (7 days)
    slope_7d = rollapply(
      sqrt(value_mean7d),
      width = 7,
      FUN = function(x) coef(lm(x ~ seq_along(x)))[2],
      fill = NA,
      align = "right"
    ),
    # phase definition
    wave_phase = case_when(
      slope_7d > 0.01 ~ "Growth",
      sqrt(value_mean7d) >= quantile(sqrt(value_mean7d), 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) ~ "High-load",
      TRUE ~ "Pre-growth"
    ),
    wave_phase = factor(
      wave_phase,
      levels = c("Pre-growth", "Growth", "High-load")
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(wave_phase))
```

```{r viral-load-by-wave-phase, fig.width=11, fig.height=6.5, dpi=300}
ggplot(
  wave_phase_df,
  aes(x = wave_phase, y = sqrt(value_mean7d), fill = wave_phase)
) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.85, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ value_category, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "wastewater viral load across wave phases",
    subtitle = "Phase definition based on short-term viral load trends",
    x = "Wave phase",
    y = expression(sqrt("value_mean7d"))
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )
```

**Interpretation**

When we look at the three phases, we can clearly see differences in viral load. Before the onset, the values are low and do not change much. During the growth phase, the viral load goes up and the wave starts to build. In the high-load phase, the values are highest and stay high for a while.

For seasonal viruses like **Influenza A**, **Influenza B** and **RSV**, this pattern is very clear and fits well with how these waves usually look. For **SARS-CoV-2**, the change between phases is slower and less sharp, which matches its more continuous circulation.

Overall, this simple phase-based view helps to describe the different parts of a wave without adding another detection step.

### Temperature by wave phase

```{r temperature-by-wave-phase, fig.width=11, fig.height=6.5, dpi=300}
ggplot(
  wave_phase_df,
  aes(x = wave_phase, y = temperature_lag7, fill = wave_phase)
) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.85, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ value_category, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Lagged temperature across wave phases",
    subtitle = "7-day lagged temperature by viral circulation phase",
    x = "Wave phase",
    y = "Temperature (°C), lagged by 7 days"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  )
```

**Interpretation**

For **Influenza A**, **Influenza B** and **RSV**, the onset phase usually happens when temperatures are lower than in the pre-onset phase. This fits with what we saw before: colder weather seems to support viral growth, especially at the beginning of a wave.

For **SARS-CoV-2**, the temperature differences between the phases are much smaller. This matches its weaker seasonal behaviour compared to the other viruses.

The results suggest that temperature is more important when seasonal viruses move from pre-onset into the onset phase. Once the viral load is already high, the influence of temperature becomes less clear.

# Forward-Looking Interpretation: Future Wave Onsets Using Past Timing Patterns

Up to this point, we only looked at what already happened in the data. We analysed how viral load changes over time, how it looks across seasons, how it is related to weather, and when wave onsets happened in the past.

In this last part, we use this information to look ahead. We do not predict exact dates. Instead, we show when during the year new waves usually start, based on what we observed before.

Because the dataset only covers two years, exact prediction models would not be reliable. For this reason, we use a simple, scenario-based approach. Past onset timings are mapped to a typical year using the day of the year. This results in time windows where new waves are more likely to begin (`onset_windows`).

The results are shown separately for each virus. This helps to describe typical onset timing and how much it varies, and to compare seasonal patterns across viruses, without claiming exact future dates.

For this analysis, we prepared the onset timing data so that each row represents the start of a detected onset zone, expressed as a day of the year.

```{r onset-timing-preparation, message=FALSE}
onset_calendar_df <- zones_all %>%
  mutate(onset_doy = yday(zone_start))
```

We summarize the onset times within one year for each virus and use this to create a time window.

```{r onset-window-definition, message=FALSE}
onset_windows <- onset_calendar_df %>%
  group_by(virus) %>%
  summarise(
    window_start = min(onset_doy),
    window_end   = max(onset_doy),
    n_onsets = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Then visualize the onset timing within a typical year.

```{r onset-window-visualization, message=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5}

virus_colors <- c(
  "Influenza A" = "#1b9e77",
  "Influenza B" = "#7570b3",
  "RSV"         = "#e7298a",
  "SARS-CoV-2"  = "#d95f02"
)

ggplot(onset_windows, aes(y = virus)) +

  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = window_start,
      xmax = window_end,
      ymin = as.numeric(factor(virus)) - 0.3,
      ymax = as.numeric(factor(virus)) + 0.3,
      fill = virus
    ),
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +

  scale_fill_manual(values = virus_colors, guide = "none") +

  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(1, 365),
    breaks = c(1, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 365),
    labels = c("Jan", "Mar", "May", "Jul", "Sep", "Nov", "Dec")
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "Plausible onset windows for wastewater viral waves",
    subtitle = "Scenario-based timing derived from past onset patterns",
    x = "Months of the year",
    y = "Virus"
  ) +

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**Interpretation**

The figure shows when viral waves usually start during the year. The windows are based on past onset timings and are shown on a typical calendar year. They do not show exact dates, but periods of the year when new waves are more likely to begin.

For **Influenza A** and **RSV**, the onset windows are clearly concentrated in late autumn and early winter. This shows a strong seasonal pattern. If future conditions are similar to those in the data, new waves for these viruses are most likely to start in this winter period. The windows are relatively narrow, which means that onset timing does not vary much between seasons.

For the other two viruses, it is not that clear: For **SARS-CoV-2**, the onset window is much broader and covers a large part of the year. This shows a weaker seasonal pattern. Wave onsets seem to be driven less by seasonal conditions. As a result, SARS-CoV-2 onsets are less predictable and not limited to one specific season.

For **Influenza B**, no clear onset window can be identified in our plot. This is because only very few onset events were detected in the data. As a result, no stable seasonal pattern can be derived for Influenza B, and no meaningful onset window can be shown.

Given the small number of detected onset events, these windows should be interpreted as illustrative rather than statistically robust estimates.

# Conclusion

This project analysed wastewater viral load data in the city of Zurich to see if weather conditions influence viral concentrations in wastewater. The analysis is limited by the relatively short observation period of two years. This restricts the ability to draw conclusions about long-term climate effects or rare extreme weather events. In addition, behavioural and epidemiological factors such as immunity levels or vaccination coverage were not included in the models. Wastewater measurements were combined with daily temperature data and rain duration data from the Ostluft platform.

The analysis showed clear seasonal patterns for Influenza A, Influenza B, and RSV. These viruses had strong peaks in winter and very low levels in summer. SARS-CoV-2 behaved differently. It was present during the whole year and showed several peaks outside the winter season. This suggests a weaker seasonal pattern.

In the exploratory analysis and the lag analysis, temperature showed a clear relationship with viral load for the seasonal viruses. Higher viral concentrations were mainly observed when temperatures were low, especially in winter. Rain duration did not show a clear relationship with viral load. This was also the case when the analysis was limited to winter months only.

To better separate seasonal effects from short-term weather effects, we used Generalized Additive Models (GAMs). The results showed that temperature mainly influences viral load within the season, but does not trigger new waves on its own (for example on cold days in summer). Rain duration did not show a stable independent effect once long-term trends over time were taken into account. For SARS-CoV-2, weather effects were generally weaker, which fits with its year-round circulation.

We also used a wave onset detection approach to identify periods of sustained viral growth before major peaks. These onset zones appeared consistently before observed outbreaks. Clear differences were visible between the seasonal viruses and SARS-CoV-2. Seasonal viruses showed compact and rather predictable onset periods in winter, while SARS-CoV-2 showed more variable onset timing across the year.

Instead of predicting exact outbreak dates, this project follows a scenario-based and period-oriented approach. With more data, additional variables, and models designed for forecasting, wastewater data could be used to define time periods when new waves are more likely to start. This is more realistic than trying to predict exact dates and could support public health monitoring and early warning systems. In practice, such period-based onset windows could support targeted preparedness planning, for example by informing testing strategies, hospital capacity planning, or public communication timing.

For the coding part of this project, ChatGPT was mainly used as a support tool. It helped with writing code and improving the visual appearance of the plots, for example by making them clearer and easier to read. The ideas, research questions, and overall structure of the analysis were developed by us. All methodological decisions and interpretations were our own. ChatGPT was also used to help with writing, language and grammar, especially when working in R Markdown, where such issues are harder to notice. In addition, it was used to check whether the structure of the R Markdown document was set up correctly, for example the order of chapters and subchapters.

Overall, this project shows that wastewater data can capture viral seasonality and epidemic dynamics well. Temperature plays an important role in increasing viral circulation during winter, while rain duration seems to have little influence. A period-based and scenario-oriented interpretation is therefore more robust than trying to predict exact future outbreak dates.
